The '''1656 Ayuman Cup''', staged at the time as the '''Ayuman Continental Tournament''' and recognised retrospectively as the 1st edition of the '''[[FLLA World Cup]]''', was the inaugural international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the leading Ayuman football associations. It was held in [[Siana]], across [[Ayuma]], from 5 June to 2 July 1656, and was won by [[Estijan]], who defeated [[Eldjo]] 6–3 in the [[#Final|final]] at the Bagusil Grand Stadium to claim the first title in the competition's history. The hosts, [[Siana]], finished third.<ref name="heritage-overview">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/overview|title=The 1656 Ayuman Cup: tournament overview|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 March 1763}}</ref>

The tournament was the first of the series later organised by the [[FLLA]] as the [[FLLA World Cup]]. It was held under the original name of the Ayuman Continental Tournament, the body of Ayuman national associations not yet having adopted the title of the Ayuman Cup that the competition would carry through its early editions; the [[FLLA]] itself, and the seven continental confederations that later structured the competition, did not yet exist, and all nine entrants were drawn from [[Ayuma]].<ref name="heritage-rename">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/history/early-competition-names|title=From the Ayuman Cup to the FLLA World Cup: the early names of the competition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1764}}</ref>

The 1656 edition was the first to be contested for the '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]]''', the original rotating trophy of the competition, which was presented to the victorious Estijani side at the close of the final. The Ayuma Cup was awarded at the first two editions, in 1656 and [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660]], before being retired in 1668 on the introduction of the original [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]]. No bespoke permanent trophy was commissioned; the permanent-trophy tradition that came to characterise the competition began only with the relaunch of the contest as the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]].<ref name="heritage-trophy">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-ayuma-cup|title=The Ayuma Cup: the original trophy of the competition, 1656 to 1668|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

==Host selection==

The first tournament was awarded to [[Siana]] by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal body that organised the competition before the foundation of the [[FLLA]]. Siana was among the prime movers behind the proposal for a continental tournament, and the congress entrusted the inaugural staging to the Sianan association on the understanding that the finals would be shared across four of its cities, with the principal matches held at the capital, [[Siana|Bagusil]]. As host nation, Siana took part automatically.<ref name="heritage-host">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/host|title=1656 Ayuman Cup: the award of hosting rights to Siana|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 March 1763}}</ref>

==Format==

The nine entered teams were divided into two groups for the group stage: a Group A of five teams and a Group B of four. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with every team playing each of the other sides in its group once; two points were awarded for a win and one for a draw, in line with the scoring system then in use. The top two teams in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]], while the remaining sides were eliminated. Where teams finished level on points, places were determined first by goal difference and then by goals scored.

The knockout stage took the form of two semi-finals, a third-place playoff and a final, each played over 90 minutes. A tie level at the end of normal time was extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; under the regulations of the period, any tie still level after extra time was to be settled by a replay rather than by a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]], a procedure not yet in use. No replay proved necessary in 1656. The two losing semi-finalists contested the third-place playoff on the day before the final.

==Participating teams==

Nine teams took part in the 1656 finals, all of them Ayuman national associations. The continental confederations that later structured the [[FLLA World Cup]] had not yet been established, and entry was settled under the informal arrangements of the period; as host nation, [[Siana]] took part automatically. The participating teams were:<ref name="heritage-teams">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/teams|title=1656 Ayuman Cup: participating teams|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 March 1763}}</ref>

==Venues==

Four stadiums in four host cities, all in [[Siana]], were used in the final tournament. The principal venue was the Bagusil Grand Stadium in the capital, [[Siana|Bagusil]], which staged the opening match and the final and was the largest ground in use. The two semi-finals were divided between the Chigao Stadium in [[Siana|Chigao]] and the Sariyah Park in [[Siana|Sariyah]], with the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] held at the Mangiwa Field in [[Siana|Mangiwa]]. The remaining group-stage fixtures were shared between the four grounds.<ref name="heritage-venues">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/venues|title=Host stadiums of the 1656 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 March 1763}}</ref>

==Squads==

Each participating association registered a squad of eighteen players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers; the smaller squads of the period reflected the limited substitution rules then in force, under which a single replacement was permitted only for an injured goalkeeper. A total of 162 players were registered for the tournament.<ref name="heritage-squads">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/squads|title=1656 Ayuman Cup: registered squads|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 March 1763}}</ref>

==Match officials==

The organising congress appointed a panel of referees and linesmen drawn from the associations not represented in the latter stages of the competition. The opening match was refereed by Halvik Marsa of [[Verusa]], and the final by Doran Vels of [[Emara]], the senior official of the tournament. The small officiating pool of the period meant that several referees took charge of fixtures involving teams from neighbouring associations, though never from their own.<ref name="heritage-officials">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/officials|title=Match officials of the 1656 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 March 1763}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The two groups were each contested as a single round-robin. The top two teams in each group advanced to the knockout stage; points were awarded on the two-points-for-a-win system in use at the time, with goal difference and then goals scored used to separate teams level on points.

All dates are given in the local time of the host cities.

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the four teams that advanced from the group stage, with each group winner drawn against the runner-up of the other group. Ties level after 90 minutes were extended by a single period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; no tie required additional time in 1656, and no replay was needed. The two losing semi-finalists contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on the day before the final.

===Final===

The final was held at the Bagusil Grand Stadium on 2 July 1656 before an estimated crowd of 13,000, the largest of the tournament. [[Estijan]] took the lead through Tomas Brody, the tournament's leading scorer, and although Halvard Renn levelled for [[Eldjo]], Emeric Sael and a second from Brody carried the side to a 3–1 advantage by the interval. Brody completed his hat-trick after the break and Lukan Verd struck twice, with a second from Renn and a late goal from Sigur Molde offering Eldjo only consolation in a 6–3 win. The victory secured the first title in the competition's history, and the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] was presented to the Estijani captain at the close of the match, the first time the trophy was awarded.<ref name="heritage-final">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/final|title=The 1656 Ayuman Cup final: Estijan 6–3 Eldjo|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 March 1763}}</ref>

==Statistics==

===Goalscorers===

A total of 119 goals were scored in 20 matches, an average of 5.95 per match. The leading scorer was the Estijani forward Tomas Brody, who scored fifteen goals across the tournament, including three in the final. No formal individual awards were presented at the 1656 edition: the leading-player, top-scorer and best-goalkeeper prizes (the [[FLLA World Cup#Awards|Vairan Ball, Marskval and Bastion]]) were not instituted until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], and the figures below are recognised retrospectively in the [[FLLA]]'s heritage records.<ref name="heritage-stats">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/statistics|title=1656 Ayuman Cup statistical record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 March 1763}}</ref>

==Trophy and significance==

The 1656 edition holds a foundational place in the history of the [[FLLA World Cup]] as the first tournament of the series and the first for which the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] was contested. Estijan's victory made the Estijani association the first champions of Ayuman international football, and the staging of the finals in [[Siana]] established the four-yearly pattern that the competition would broadly keep through its early editions.<ref name="heritage-overview" />

The cup that Estijan lifted was the Ayuma Cup, which was contested again at the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660 edition]] before being retired in 1668 on the introduction of the original [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]]. The Ayuma Cup survives as the oldest senior trophy in the [[FLLA]] system; it was the original Andah Cup, the trophy used from 1668, that was lost when it remained in [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]] and was destroyed there at the outbreak of the [[Red War]] in 1688. When the competition was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], no rotating cup was available, and the host association instead commissioned a bespoke permanent trophy, beginning the permanent-trophy tradition that has characterised the competition ever since.<ref name="heritage-trophy" />

The success of the inaugural tournament encouraged the Ayuman national associations to repeat the contest, and a second edition followed in [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660]]. The competition would be staged among Ayuman nations under the Ayuman Cup name until the foundation of the [[FLLA]] opened it to the wider game.<ref name="heritage-rename" />
